plan: Applied the verbal anti-tell checklist: moderate wrong choices, paraphrased keys, balanced lengths. Literary purpose, two-part data claim, trade-contact inference, along-with agreement, colon-list, cross-text partial-concession trap; S009-04 resubmitted.

passages.title: Novelist prose
passages.text: The novelist's prose is famously ______: a single sentence may run for a full page, looping through memories and side remarks before it finally returns to its subject.

passages.title: City nights
passages.text:
The following text is from a short story. Inés has recently moved from her grandmother's rural home to a city apartment.
At night the building was never quiet. Pipes knocked in the walls, a neighbor's television murmured through the floor, and the elevator groaned between stories. Inés had expected to find the noise unbearable. Instead, lying awake on the third night, she realized she had been listening for it, the way she had once listened for the creek behind her grandmother's house.

passages.title: Irrigation yields
passages.text:
A researcher measured yields of three crops, in units per plot, with and without irrigation.
Crop | Without irrigation | With irrigation
Wheat | 30 | 42
Barley | 25 | 41
Oats | 28 | 36
The researcher claimed that the crop with the greatest increase from irrigation was also the crop with the lowest yield without irrigation.

passages.title: Two valleys
passages.text: Linguists studying a language spoken in two neighboring valleys found that speakers in the eastern valley use a word for "river" borrowed from a neighboring language, while speakers in the western valley use an older native word. Historical records show that the eastern valley was a regional trading center for centuries, while the western valley was relatively isolated. These findings suggest that ______

passages.title: Mayor visit
passages.text: The mayor, along with three members of the city council and two engineers from the state transportation department, ______ scheduled to tour the flooded neighborhood on Monday morning.

passages.title: Tool kit
passages.text: The basic repair kit sold at the hardware store includes several ______ a wrench, a level, a utility knife, and a twenty-five-foot tape measure.

passages.title: Early telescopes
passages.text: Early telescopes produced blurry images because different colors of light passing through a lens came into focus at slightly different points. ______ astronomers often had to choose between a bright image and a sharp one, since reducing the blur also meant letting in less light.

passages.title: Glacier notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Glaciers in the Arven Range have lost about 40% of their area since 1950.
• Average summer temperatures there have risen by 1.5°C over the same period.
• Researchers attribute most of the glacier loss to longer melt seasons.
• Melt seasons in the range now begin about three weeks earlier than in 1950.

passages.title: Bike lanes (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
A downtown business owner argues that replacing street parking with bike lanes will hurt local shops, because most customers arrive by car and will go elsewhere if they cannot park.

Text 2
Studies of similar changes in several cities found that shop revenue on affected streets usually rose. Cyclists tended to spend somewhat less per visit than drivers, but they visited more often.

passages.title: Learning grammar (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
A linguist argues that young children learn the grammar of their first language mainly because adults correct their grammatical mistakes.

Text 2
Researchers who recorded hundreds of hours of conversation between parents and young children found that parents rarely corrected grammatical errors; they usually corrected statements that were factually wrong instead. The children nevertheless acquired their language's grammar on a typical schedule.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: looping through memories and side remarks before it finally returns to its subject
candidates.explanation: Prose that wanders through digressions before returning to its subject is "discursive."

A.rationale: Terse prose is brief, the opposite of page-long sentences.

B.rationale: Lucid means clear; the colon describes wandering length, not clarity.

D.rationale: Formulaic means predictable; looping digressions are not a formula.

hints: What does the colon clause describe?
candidates.remember: Use the colon clause to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe in detail the problems with the building's old plumbing
choices.B: To show a character beginning to find comfort in an unfamiliar place
choices.C: To suggest that Inés deeply regrets leaving her grandmother's home
choices.D: To explain the reasons Inés decided to move from the country

candidates.evidence: she realized she had been listening for it
candidates.explanation: Ines expected the noise to be unbearable but finds herself listening for it, as she once listened for the creek: the noise has become comforting.

A.rationale: The noises are details serving the character's realization, not the focus.

C.rationale: The creek memory is a comparison showing comfort, not regret.

D.rationale: Her reasons for moving are never given.

hints: What did Inés expect, and what happened instead?

strategy.explanation: State the turn in one sentence.

candidates.remember: In literary texts, look for the character's change.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's claim?

choices.A: Wheat had the highest unirrigated yield, 30 units, and reached 42 with irrigation.
choices.B: Oats gained only 8 units with irrigation, the smallest increase of the three crops.
choices.C: Barley reached 41 units with irrigation, nearly matching wheat's 42 units.
choices.D: Barley had the lowest unirrigated yield, 25 units, and gained the most, 16 units.

candidates.evidence: the crop with the greatest increase from irrigation was also the crop with the lowest yield without irrigation
candidates.explanation: Gains: wheat 12, barley 16, oats 8. Barley has both the largest gain and the lowest unirrigated yield (25), which is exactly the claim.

A.rationale: Wheat is not the crop the claim describes.

B.rationale: This concerns the smallest gain, not the claim about the largest.

C.rationale: This compares irrigated yields, not gains or unirrigated yields.

hints: Which crop is lowest without irrigation?

strategy.explanation: Turn the claim into two checks.

candidates.remember: A two-part claim needs both parts shown.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: contact through trade may help explain why the eastern valley adopted the borrowed word.
choices.B: western speakers were simply unfamiliar with the neighboring language's word for "river."
choices.C: the borrowed word for "river" is older than the native word still used in the west.
choices.D: most of the trade in the eastern valley involved goods carried along its rivers.

candidates.evidence: the eastern valley was a regional trading center for centuries
candidates.explanation: The valley with long trade contact uses the borrowed word; the isolated valley keeps the native one. Contact through trade plausibly explains the borrowing.

B.rationale: Possible, but the text gives no evidence about what western speakers knew.

C.rationale: The text calls the native word "older."

D.rationale: The kind of goods traded is never discussed.

hints: What differs between the valleys' histories?
Which difference matches the word difference?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices the text does not support.

candidates.remember: Link the difference in outcomes to the difference in conditions.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The mayor, along with three members
candidates.explanation: Phrases beginning with "along with" are set off by commas and do not change the number of the subject. "The mayor" is singular: "is."

A.rationale: "Along with ..." does not make the subject plural; the subject is "the mayor."

C.rationale: "Were" is plural and shifts to the past tense.

hints: Which noun comes right before the first comma?
candidates.remember: "Along with" phrases don't make a subject plural.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: "The basic repair kit ... includes several tools" is a complete clause, so a colon can introduce the list that follows.

B.rationale: A colon should not follow "such as."

C.rationale: A colon should not follow "such as."

D.rationale: A semicolon cannot introduce a list.

hints: Is the part before the blank a complete sentence?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate colons after "such as" and semicolons before lists.

candidates.remember: A colon introduces a list only after a complete clause.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.explanation: The color blur forced a tradeoff between brightness and sharpness: a consequence, so "As a result."

A.rationale: The second sentence follows from the first rather than contrasting with it.

B.rationale: The tradeoff is a consequence of the blur, not an instance of it.

D.rationale: "Nevertheless" would suggest astronomers acted despite the problem, not because of it.

hints: Does the second sentence follow from or contrast with the first?

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain why the Arven Range glaciers have shrunk. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: According to researchers, glaciers in the Arven Range have lost about 40% of their area since 1950.
choices.B: Researchers attribute most of the glacier loss to melt seasons that start three weeks earlier.
choices.C: Average summer temperatures in the Arven Range have risen by 1.5°C since 1950.
choices.D: In the Arven Range, melt seasons now begin about three weeks earlier than they did in 1950.

candidates.evidence: Researchers attribute most of the glacier loss to longer melt seasons.
candidates.explanation: Only B links a cause (longer melt seasons, starting three weeks earlier) to the effect (glacier shrinkage).

A.rationale: This states the effect without giving a cause.

C.rationale: This is related, but it never connects warming to the glaciers.

D.rationale: This gives the change but does not link it to glacier loss.

hints: Which choice connects a cause to the glaciers?

strategy.explanation: An explanation must link cause and effect.

candidates.remember: Explanations connect a cause to its effect explicitly.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the business owner's prediction in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the change will reduce revenue because cyclists spend less per visit
choices.B: By arguing that most downtown customers already arrive by bicycle rather than by car
choices.C: By claiming that the owner's shop sells goods that cyclists rarely want to buy
choices.D: By noting that the prediction overlooks how often cyclists return to shop

candidates.explanation: The owner assumes losing drivers means losing revenue. Text 2 reports revenue rose because cyclists, though spending less per visit, came more often, which is the factor the owner ignores.

A.rationale: Text 2 grants lower spending per visit but reports that revenue usually rose.

B.rationale: Text 2 says nothing about how most customers currently arrive.

C.rationale: Text 2 does not discuss any particular shop or product.

hints: What does Text 2 say makes up for lower spending?
candidates.remember: A partial concession is not agreement with the conclusion.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the linguist's claim in Text 1?

choices.A: By noting that children master grammar even though they seldom receive the correction the claim relies on
choices.B: By conceding that corrections help, though less than Text 1 assumes
choices.C: By arguing that correcting a child's factual errors is more harmful than correcting grammar
choices.D: By suggesting that children who are corrected more often learn grammar more slowly than others

candidates.explanation: If grammatical corrections are rare yet children still learn grammar on schedule, correction cannot be the main mechanism, contradicting Text 1.

B.rationale: Text 2 reports that grammatical corrections were rare, not that they helped somewhat; it gives no evidence that they help at all.

C.rationale: Text 2 makes no claim about harm.

D.rationale: Text 2 does not compare children by how often they are corrected.

hints: What does Text 1 say causes grammar learning?
How common is that cause, according to Text 2?

strategy.explanation: Compare the claimed cause with the observed frequency.

candidates.remember: If the supposed cause is rare, the effect needs another explanation.
candidates.revision_note: S009-04 resubmitted: relabelled easy (both raters about 80%); choice B rewritten as a moderate near-miss so the key is no longer the only non-extreme option.
